extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and informed readers of political theory and public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative principles and practical criteria implied by democratic theory and constitutional design as discussed in a political-philosophical text. Focuses on how public opinion, representation, institutional design, and administrative practice affect the functioning of democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneous democracy and confined informational environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy as an ideal presumes people "managed their own affairs spontaneously" and that the environment of democratic action be "confined within the range of every man's direct and certain knowledge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains this ideal arises from small, self-governing townships and implies that for democracy to be 'spontaneous' interests must remain simple, intelligible, and easily managed. When the environment is wide and unpredictable, the democratic stereotype struggles; contacts outside the self-contained group are seen as threats. Anti-patterns: assuming ordinary voters can reliably form opinions about distant or complex affairs without adequate instruments of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency as a democratic premise
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic ideal emphasized "self-sufficiency" and avoidance of entanglement — an aim to "achieve self-sufficiency and avoid entanglement" within protected boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to foreign-policy tendencies like splendid isolation or doctrines (Monroe Doctrine) meant to supplement geographic security. The text links self-sufficiency to limits on manufactures, foreign commerce, and external relations. Practical consequence: democratic preferences often favor policies that make the polity appear self-contained even when unrealistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the omnicompetent citizen
rubrics_metrics.description: Democrats assumed "one man was as competent as the next to manage these simple and self-contained affairs" — the idea of the omnicompetent citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the rural township this is often true (rotation in office, jack-of-all-trades). But universal application to a complex civilization is a category error: it produces problems when applied to national policymaking. Anti-pattern: treating complex national administration as if any citizen can immediately perform competently without specialization or institutional supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous moral/code assumption for effective public reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: In a self-contained community "one could assume... a homogeneous code of morals" so disagreements would be confined to logical application of accepted standards to accepted facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues this assumption undergirds confidence that free discussion yields truth locally. But where codes and facts are not common, this premise fails and public opinion becomes fragmented and stereotype-driven. Implication: democratic legitimacy is fragile when the shared moral/informational base is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimization of the unseen environment ("the mirror is concave")
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic theory historically "minimize[d] the importance of that unseen environment" because decisions about unfamiliar external affairs are "manifestly settled at haphazard."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cognitive tendency drives distrust of foreign trade, manufactures, and large-scale organizations; it motivates utopian retreat to isolated communities. Practical warning: democracies that ignore complex, unseen forces risk making haphazard decisions on matters requiring expert knowledge and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insecurity/crisis danger incompatible with mass democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every democrat feels in his bones that dangerous crises are incompatible with democracy," because rapid action often requires decisions by a few rather than mass deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains inertia of masses forces quick decisions to be made by a small number, which threatens democratic ideals. Consequence: democracies prefer pacifist or defensive wars and fear surprises. Institutional implication: need for structures that can handle emergencies without sacrificing democratic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances to neutralize local opinion (ambition vs ambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To govern a large heterogeneous polity the framers relied on institutional devices so that "Ambition... must be made to counteract ambition" and to "enable the government to control the governed, and in the next place, oblige it to control itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks and balances were conceived as a remedy to local self-centeredness and to prevent local interests from obstructing national government. The text stresses this was a conscious device to substitute institutional 'mild influence' for brute force. Limitation: the device was intended to deadlock local and class interests, not to produce perpetual paralysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional informational deficiency: representatives as 'blind men'
rubrics_metrics.description: A "congress of representatives is essentially a group of blind men in a vast, unknown world" because the constitutional theory supplied no systematic, adequate, authorized method for Congress to know what is going on in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues Congress's only recognized method is exchanging district opinions, which is insufficient for national and foreign policy. Practical remedy: Congress needs instruments of controlled reporting and objective analysis; without them legislation either is made by a few insiders or broken into local items. Anti-patterns: relying solely on local impressions or partisan 'tips' for complex policy judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for controlled reporting and objective analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers "need to know the local pictures, but unless he possesses instruments for calibrating them, one picture is as good as the next" — hence the need for controlled reporting and objective analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogized to a factory head needing cost sheets and accountants, legislators require systematically prepared information. The text cites positive developments: occasional use of expert bodies (Interstate Commerce Commission, Federal Trade Commission, Tariff Commission) to provide data and analysis. Recommendation: institutionalize analytic capacities to inform national policy rather than rely on ad hoc or partisan sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive informational advantage and asymmetric relationship with Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: The President, who "presides over a vast collection of bureaus and their agents," can present to Congress what he chooses; "He tells Congress what he chooses to tell it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a one-sided relationship allowing censorship and selective disclosure, contributing to an informational imbalance. Consequence: Congress may be forced to rely on newspapers, leaks, or investigations to obtain needed documents. Institutional implication: checks to ensure Congress access to unbiased information are necessary to preserve balanced policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional investigations as a flawed substitute for routine information
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress is starved of legitimate information, it resorts to "that legalized atrocity, the Congressional investigation," where members "go on a wild and feverish man-hunt."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations are depicted as an imperfect, often sensational method of acquiring information and lack the regularity and objectivity of systematic reporting. They are costly and politically fraught, and yield little routine policy insight. Recommendation: build regular, nonpartisan information channels instead of relying on episodic investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logrolling and localism in legislative production
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature without effective means of information "must oscillate between blind regularity... and logrolling," and legislation becomes a collection of local items (tariff schedules, navy yards, post offices) "fed out to concave communities as tangible evidence of the benefits of national life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because representatives best understand local effects, national legislation is often parcelled into local benefits exchanged by logrolling. This obscures cumulative costs and undermines coherent national policymaking. Anti-pattern: accepting pork-barrel bundling as the norm rather than seeking analytic aggregation of translocal impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage and rotation in office as democratic instrument with unintended consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotation in office and short terms were seen as a democratic reform to prevent bureaucratic monopoly, but in practice patronage "founded a new governing class" and produced a permanent professional politician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While rotation acknowledged the dignity of the average man and aimed to open careers, it unintentionally created party machines and a governing class. The text notes patronage nonetheless contributed to governmental stability by binding leaders to national interests. Practical lesson: reforms intended to democratize access to office can have perverse institutional effects; anticipate and mitigate professionalization and machine politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption that only affairs of universal interest are important
rubrics_metrics.description: Because "only those affairs came to seem important in which everybody was interested," democrats tended to view importance through what engaged the whole community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cognitive filter leads to neglect of specialized or technical public matters that do not arouse broad popular interest, leaving such issues under-addressed. Policy implication: mechanisms are needed to surface and translate specialized but important issues for broad democratic consideration.
